candidates.title: Red Sea returns are rewriting carrier reliability, not just transit times
candidates.excerpt: The return of container services to the Red Sea is changing Asia–Europe schedules again. For shippers preparing 2027 contracts, the attraction is clear: Suez offers a shorter route than the Cape of Good Hope. The harder question is whether the shorter passage will produce more dependable arrival windows. The transition is taking place service by service. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd moved their joint ME1 service, linking India and Europe, to the trans-Suez route from November, with the first westbound and eastbound sailings scheduled from Salalah on 4 November and Tangier on 13 November. On 17 November, Hapag-Lloyd announced that three further Gemini services, NE1, NE2 and NE3, would also return to Suez, with initial westbound transitions scheduled for December 2026 and January 2027. The sequence shows that the return is being managed through individual service decisions, not a single network-wide switch. For cargo owners, this distinction matters. candidates.title: Napier Port lifts earnings despite flat container volumes
candidates.excerpt: Napier Port reported further earnings growth for the financial year ended 30 September 2026, supported by a stronger cargo mix, higher container revenue and its yield-management strategy. Revenue increased by 11.7% to NZ$176.2 million, compared with NZ$157.7 million in the previous financial year. Reported net profit after tax rose by 15% to NZ$35.5 million. Underlying net profit increased by 30.5% to NZ$36.9 million. The port’s result from operating activities reached NZ$75.7 million, representing an increase of 17.9%. Its operating margin improved from 40.7% to 43%. “2026 was a strong year of service delivery and continued earnings growth for Napier Port,” said Blair O’Keeffe, Chair of Napier Port. “The result reflects the strength of our diverse cargo base, continued progress with our yield and cost management strategies, and the resilience of Hawke’s Bay’s primary sector,” he added. candidates.title: DP World completes Posorja terminal expansion
candidates.excerpt: DP World has completed the latest expansion of its deep-water container terminal in Posorja, Ecuador, extending the berth to 800 metres and increasing annual handling capacity to 1.4 million TEU. The development forms part of a privately funded investment of more than US$200 million. It is intended to accommodate larger vessels, improve terminal efficiency and strengthen Ecuador’s connections with international markets. The latest work follows the completion of a 700-metre berth earlier in 2026. New cranes to enter service in 2027 DP World has also added a fully electric quay crane and three hybrid rubber-tyred gantry cranes at Posorja. The new quay crane is 56 metres high and has a reach of 72 metres. It can serve container vessels measuring up to 400 metres in length, with capacities ranging from 20,000 to 24,000 TEU. candidates.title: Stamford firms up 10 MR tankers in China
candidates.excerpt: Singapore-based Stamford Shipping has firmed up an order for 10 MR product tankers at China’s Nantong CIMC Sinopacific Offshore & Engineering (CIMC SOE), with the yard also securing two vessels of the same design from an unidentified European owner. The shipbuilder, part of Hong Kong-listed CIMC Enric, has confirmed that construction contracts covering all 12 ships are now effective, according to a Chinese shipbuilding industry report published on November 16. Each vessel will have a capacity of 49,900 dwt, giving the combined order a total of nearly 600,000 dwt. No contract value, construction timetable or delivery schedule has been disclosed. The deal marks the yard’s entry into the MR product tanker segment, adding a new vessel type to a portfolio dominated by LNG bunkering ships, LPG and ammonia carriers, and feeder containerships. candidates.title: ECB to step up scrutiny of banks’ private credit exposures
candidates.excerpt: ECB to step up scrutiny of banks’ private credit exposures The European Central Bank (ECB) is planning to step up its scrutiny of banks’ exposure to private credit funds and other non-bank financial institutions amid concerns about risk management and growing interconnectedness. In its supervisory priorities for 2027–29, published today (19 November), the ECB outlined plans for a new campaign of on-site inspections covering fund financing, asset-based lending and exposures to non-bank financial institutions. The inspections will focus particularly on banks’ relationships with private equity, private credit and funds investing in tangible assets. The regulator warned that banks’ growing links to non-bank financial institutions could increase risks during periods of market stress, particularly where counterparties have higher levels of risk. candidates.title: Finom launches new credit products for SMEs in Germany and Netherlands
candidates.excerpt: Finom launches new credit products for SMEs in Germany and Netherlands European financial platform Finom has launched two new credit products for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Germany and the Netherlands, as it looks to address a gap in short-term business financing. The Amsterdam-based fintech business, which serves 300,000 businesses, has introduced a business overdraft and credit card, offering personalised limits of up to €20,000 (£16,700) and €40,000, respectively. The products use customers’ existing transaction data to make credit decisions in seconds, removing the need for businesses to submit annual accounts or bank statements. Finom said more than half of its customers now qualify for credit under the new offering, compared with between 11 per cent and 17 per cent under its previous credit product. Technology companies now account for around 25 per cent of the fund’s deployed capital. candidates.excerpt: WASHINGTON — U.S. weekly rail traffic again showed a solid increase over 2025 levels for the week ending Nov. 14, 2026, thanks to the continued strength of intermodal volume. According to the Association of American Railroads, traffic for the week was 529,919 carloads and intermodal units, up 7.3% from the same week a year ago. That included 230,260 carloads, a gain of 3.3%, and 299,659 intermodal units, up 10.7%. Through 45 weeks of 2026, total combined traffic is 23,171,466 carloads and intermodal units, an increase of 4% compared with the same period last year. The overall figure includes 10,301,533 carloads, up 2.7%, and 12,869,933 intermodal units, up 5%. North American traffic for the week, as reported by nine U.S., Canadian, and Mexican railroads, included 728,661 carloads and intermodal units, an increase of 7.2% from the same week in 2025.
